Customize your light fixture switches with this easy guide
A 3-way switch allows you to turn a light on or off from two different switches. 3-way switches are useful for large rooms with multiple entrances but require a bit more wiring than a standard, single-pole switch. The wiring method will depend on whether your power goes to the switch first or the light first.
[[Category:Electrical Wiring and Safety Switches]]
==3-Way Switch Wiring: Overview ==
#Turn off the circuit and run two 2-wire conductors between the 2 electrical boxes.
#Run a black wire from the new 3-way switch to the power source.
#Connect another black wire from the light to the original switch location.
#Cap the white neutral wires to both switch boxes.
#Connect the traveler wires using the bottom conductor.
#Cap the equipment grounding conductors together at each switch and the light.
#Replace the switch box covers and test your new 3-way switch.
==Steps==
===Taking Safety Precautions{{toc_item:Safety & Setup}}===

#Switch off the circuit. Ensure that the circuit for the room you are working in has been flipped off. This will prevent accidental electrocution and reduce the risk of fire.<ref>https://www.cnet.com/how-to/how-to-replace-3-way-light-switch/</ref>[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Most circuit breakers are located in the garage or basement, but placement will vary from home to home.

#*When you find the breaker box, locate the breaker that controls the lights for the room you are working on. Flip it to the off position to keep power from traveling down those wires. Most electrical panels label switches for the different rooms in your home.
#*[[Use-Voltage-Testers|Use a voltage tester]] to check that power is no longer flowing to that room.

#Determine if the power goes to the light or the light switch. This will affect the way that you perform the installation. You can tell if the power is coming into the switch by removing the light switch panel. If two black wires are coming into the switch box, then the power is coming into the switch first. If there is only one black wire, then the power is coming into the switch from the light fixture. You can usually use an electrical tester to be sure.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 2 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Replace any regular switches with the 3-way switches. A 3-way switch will not have the words on or off written on it. Before you start installing, take a look at your new 3-way switch to identify all of the terminals that you will be connecting wires to.<ref>https://www.how-to-wire-it.com/how-to-wire-a-3-way-switch.html</ref>[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 3 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Traveler wire terminals - These are located on each side of the switch towards the top of the switch.<ref>https://www.how-to-wire-it.com/how-to-wire-a-3-way-switch.html</ref>

#*Ground wire terminal - Older switches may not have this, but all new switches must. This is usually a green screw located on the top or bottom of the switch, mounted to the frame. <ref>https://www.how-to-wire-it.com/how-to-wire-a-3-way-switch.html</ref>
#*Common wire screw - This is located on the left side of the switch, and is a different color than the two traveler terminals.

#Install larger electrical boxes. You will likely need larger boxes than you already have if you are replacing a regular single-pole switch. 3-way switches involve more cables, so you will need a little more room to work.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Run 2 2-wire conductors between the two boxes. Choose 14-2 or 12-2 NM cable, depending on the breaker.<ref>https://www.familyhandyman.com/electrical/wiring-switches/how-to-wire-a-threeway-switch/</ref> 14 gauge wire needs a 15 amp breaker, while a 12 gauge wire requires a 20 amp breaker. You’ll be using the top conductor to run your hot wires and your neutrals while the bottom conductor will be used for your traveler wires.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 5 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*See [[Fish-Wires-Through-Walls|this guide]] for details on running wire through your wall.
#*The first number specifies the gauge and the second number is the number of wires carrying current.
#*You may also use a single 14/3 or 12/3 cable, which contains 1 bare ground wire, 1 white wire, 1 black wire, and 1 red wire.

#*If the power comes from the light’s location, run the 2-wire conductors up from each switch to the light fixture. Many of the conductor connections will be made in the light’s device box, so make sure you have enough room for all the wires.
===Converting a Single-Pole Switch to a 3-Way{{toc_item:Converting a Switch}}===

#Run a black wire from the new switch to the power source. Use the black wire in the top 2-wire conductor to attach the switch to the source. Make a J-hook in the wire with a pair of pliers and wrap it around the black common screw on the light switch. Tighten the screw to secure it in place. Cap the wires connecting the source and the switch. [[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*The screw is typically on the bottom of the switch.
#*Don’t attach the traveler wires to the common screw since they’re only used to connect the switches together.

#Connect another black wire from the light to the original switch location. Use the existing 2-wire conductor leading from the light to the switch. Attach the wire to the black common screw on the switch. [[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 7 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Make sure you don’t attach the traveler wires to the common screw, or else the switches won’t work properly.

#Cap the white neutral wires to each switch box. Place a plastic cap on the end of the white wire from the top conductor in the new switch location. Take the neutrals from the other end of the top conductor, the power source, and the light and cap them in the original switch location.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 8 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Neutrals need to be in place at every switch box according to the NEC 2017 electrical code. Older homes may not have neutrals in the switch boxes. It is okay to replace switches in this instance.

#*If you install smart switches, the neutral will attach to them and make it work. If there isn’t a neutral wire in the switch box, you have to run one from another location before installing the smart switch.

#Connect the traveler wires using the bottom conductor. Use the black and white cables from the bottom conductor to attach the traveler terminals on each switch. It doesn’t matter which terminals they are attached to on each switch. Use a pair of pliers to bend the exposed ends of the wire around each screw.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 9 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Mark the white traveler cable with a black piece of electric tape so you know that the wire is hot.
#*If you’re using a 12/3 or 14/3 cable, use the black and red wires as your travelers.

#Cap the equipment grounding conductors together at each switch and the light. Find the grounding screw on the top or bottom of each of the switches. Wrap the wires tightly around the screw and use a screwdriver to tighten the screws.  Cap the grounding conductors at each switch box. Push the wires into the back of your box.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Make sure you ground both switches, or else they may not be safe.
#*If your switch boxes are made of metal, the grounding conductor needs to bond to them as well.

#Replace the switch box covers. Screw the switches into the electrical box and secure the wall plate over the opening. Flip the breakers back on and test the switches.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]
==Tips==
*According to the 2017 National Electric Code (NEC), a neutral is required at each 3-way switch location to complete the circuit.
== Warnings ==
* Always make sure the power to the area where you are working is off to avoid electrocution.
* Call a licensed electrician if the wiring in your house is aluminum. The inside of the coating will be light gray instead of copper. You should not work on it yourself.
== Things You'll Need ==
* 14-2 or 12-2 wire cable
* 3-way switches
* Voltage tester (non-contact)
* Screwdriver
* Needle-nose pliers
* Wire stripper
* Black electrical tape
* Utility knife

#Replace any regular switches with the 3-way switches. A 3-way switch will not have the words on or off written on it. Before you start installing, take a look at your new 3-way switch to identify all of the terminals that you will be connecting wires to.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Run 2 2-wire conductors between the two boxes. Choose 14-2 or 12-2 NM cable, depending on the breaker. 14 gauge wire needs a 15 amp breaker, while a 12 gauge wire requires a 20 amp breaker. You’ll be using the top conductor to run your hot wires and your neutrals while the bottom conductor will be used for your traveler wires.
#*The first number specifies the gauge and the second number is the number of wires carrying current.

#*If the power comes from the light’s location, run the 2-wire conductors up from each switch to the light fixture. Many of the conductor connections will be made in the light’s device box, so make sure you have enough room for all the wires.
===Converting a Single-Pole Switch to a 3-Way===

#Run a black wire from the new switch to the power source. Use the black wire in the top 2-wire conductor to attach the switch to the source. Make a J-hook in the wire with a pair of pliers and wrap it around the black screw on the light switch. Tighten the screw to secure it in place. Cap the wires connecting the source and the switch.
#*The screw is typically on the bottom of the switch.
#Connect another black wire from the light to the original switch location. Use the existing 2-wire conductor leading from the light to the switch. Attach the wire to the black screw on the switch.

#Cap the white neutral wires to each switch box. Place a plastic cap on the end of the white wire from the top conductor in the new switch location. Take the neutrals from the other end of the top conductor, the power source, and the light and cap them in the original switch location.
#*Neutrals need to be in place at every switch box according to the NEC 2017 electrical code. Older homes may not have neutrals in the switch boxes. It is okay to replace switches in this instance.
#*If you install smart switches, the neutral will attach to them and make it work.

#Connect the traveler wires using the bottom conductor. Use the black and white cables from the bottom conductor to attach the traveler terminals on each switch. It doesn’t matter which terminals they are attached to on each switch. Use a pair of pliers to bend the exposed ends of the wire around each screw.
#*Mark the white traveler cable with a black piece of electric tape so you know that the wire is hot.

#Cap the equipment grounding conductors together at each switch and the light. Find the grounding screw on the top or bottom of each of the switches. Wrap the wires tightly around the screw and use a screwdriver to tighten the screws.  Cap the grounding conductors at each switch box. Push the wires into the back of your box.
#*If your switch box is made of metal, the grounding conductor needs to bond to the box as well.
#Replace the switch box covers. Screw the switches into the electrical box and secure the wall plate over the opening. Flip the breakers back on and test the switches.
==Tips==

*According to the 2017 National Electric Code (NEC), a neutral is required at each 3-way switch location. This helps ground the switch if new smart switches are present.<ref>http://www.ncdoi.com/OSFM/Engineering_and_Codes/Documents/2017%20Amendments%20to%20be%20adopted%20with%20the%20NEC%20Version%201.pdf</ref>
* 14-2 or 12-2 wire cable

According to the 2017 National Electric Code (NEC), a neutral is required at each 3 way switch location.<ref>http://www.ncdoi.com/OSFM/Engineering_and_Codes/Documents/2017%20Amendments%20to%20be%20adopted%20with%20the%20NEC%20Version%201.pdf</ref> This helps ground the switch if new smart technology is present. Call an electrician to run wires to each electrical box that you plan to attach for a 3 way switch.<ref>https://youtu.be/_no-E8ZOkfQ?t=9m12s</ref>
#*If neutrals are present in your electrical box already, attach them to the neutral running from the fixture by twisting the wires and cover the exposed ends of the wire with a wire cap.

#Run the 3-wire cable between the two boxes. Choose 14-3 or 12-3 NM cable, depending on the breaker. 14 gauge wire needs a 15 amp breaker, while a 12 gauge wire requires a 20 amp breaker. You must use this type of cable to ensure correct voltage and the number of wires.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*The first number specifies the gauge and the second number is the number of wires carrying current. A cable for a 3-way will have 3 insulated wires: black, red, and white.
===Installing a New 3 Way Switch===

#Wire a black common wire from the line source to the first switch. Make a J-hook in the wire with a pair of pliers and wrap it around the black screw on the light switch. Tighten the screw to secure it in place.<ref>https://youtu.be/U3H6kzBfOgc?t=3m38s</ref>

#Attach a common wire from the light to the terminal on the second switch. Take the black wire from the light fixture and attach it to the black screw on the second switch.<ref>https://youtu.be/U3H6kzBfOgc?t=5m49s</ref>

#Connect the red traveler wires to a traveler terminal on each switch. It doesn’t matter which traveler terminal the wires are connected to on each switch. Use a pair of pliers to bend the exposed ends of the wire into hooks and wrap them around the terminals.<ref>https://youtu.be/BkLL0J07WsQ?t=5m11s</ref>

#Attach the other traveler wire to the second traveler terminal of each switch. This wire is typically black, but the color could vary dependant on how your house is wired. Connect the traveler wire between the 2 switches on the open terminals.<ref>https://youtu.be/BkLL0J07WsQ?t=5m11s</ref>

#Connect the ground wires to the grounding screw on each switch. Find the grounding screw on the top or bottom of each of the switches. Wrap the wires tightly around the screw and use a screwdriver to tighten the screws. Push the wires into the back of your box.<ref>https://youtu.be/U3H6kzBfOgc?t=6m9s</ref>

#Cap the neutral wires between the line source and the light at each box. Twist the white neutral wires with a pair of pliers in each switch box. Twist a wire cap onto the exposed ends. If you ever install smart light switches, you’ll use the neutral wires.<ref>https://youtu.be/U3H6kzBfOgc?t=3m55s</ref>
#*Neutrals need to be in place at every switch box according to the NEC 2017 electrical code.

#Replace the switch box cover. Screw the switches into the electrical box and secure the wall plate over the opening. Flip the breakers back on and test the switches.

#Wire the common terminals for each switch. Connect the black wire from the power source to the common terminal of the first switch. Connect the black wire from the new cable to the common terminal on the second switch.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Connect the white travelers. Connect the white wire at each end of the new cable to the travel terminal on the right side of the switch. Mark this wire with black tape to indicate that it is "hot" (white wires usually aren't).[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Connect the red travelers. Connect the red travelers to the left traveler terminals on each switch.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Attach the ground wire on the second switch. Use the ground wire from the new cable.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Connect the old white wire to the existing cable headed to the light. When you pulled out your old switch, there was a white wire attached. Connect this white wire to the white wire that is connected to the light. Use a wire nut to connect them. Consult your local electrician or hardware store to ensure you’re using the proper size wire nut for your set up.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Connect the black wire from the light to the new cable. This black wire used to be attached to the old switch, and runs directly to the light. Connect this to the black wire in the new cable, on the first switch end. Use a wire nut to connect them.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 11.jpg|center]]

#Ground the first switch. Connect the ground wire from the power source, the ground wire to the light, and the ground wire from the new cable to the ground terminal on the first switch. Use a wire nut to connect them all.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 12.jpg|center]]

#Install the switches. Now that both switches have been wired, you can screw them into the electrical boxes installed in the wall. Turn the breaker back on, and then give the switches a test.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 13.jpg|center]]
===Replacing Switches If Power Runs to the Fixture===

#Connect the power to the new cable. Since the power comes from the light, you will need to transfer this power to the second switch. Connect the black wire from the light to the black wire on the new cable in the original switch box. Use a wire nut to connect them.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 14.jpg|center]]

#Wire the common terminals. Connect the white wire from the light to the common terminal on the first switch. Mark the wire with electrical tape to indicate that it is hot. Connect the black wire from the new cable to the common terminal on the second switch.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 15.jpg|center]]

#Wire the traveler terminals. Connect the white wire on both ends of the new cable to the left traveler terminals on each switch. Mark them with electrical tape to indicate that they are hot. Connect the red wire on both ends of the new cable to the right traveler terminals on each switch.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 16.jpg|center]]

#Ground the switches. Connect the ground wire from the new cable to the ground terminal on the second switch. Connect the ground wire from the new cable and the power cable from the light with a wire nut. Make sure the nut is fastened securely. Connect these to the ground terminal on the first switch.[[Image:Wire a 3 Way Switch Step 17.jpg|center]]

Using 3-way switches in houses allows you to turn off a light from 2 different outlets. Wiring these switches can be trickier than the typical single switch, but, once it is done, it can add the convenience of controlling lights from multiple places. This article will tell you how to wire a 3-way switch.
== Steps ==
# Turn off the power to the correct circuit from your power panel. Ensure you have a new electrical box for one of your 3-way switches and a larger box in place of the old switch.
# Feed 14-3 or 12-3 NM cable between the two boxes. You must use this type of cable to ensure correct voltage and the number of wires.
#* The first number specifies the gauge and the second number is the number of wires carrying current. A cable for a 3-way will have insulated wires: black, red, and white.
# Make sure the power is off to the room by using a voltage tester before continuing. You will have to strip the ends of the wires to expose the copper center.

#* Connect the wires to the new switches. The exact connection varies according to the type of setup in your house. The most common setup is where the power coming in goes to your light switch first. The other setup is when the power goes to your light fixture first.

# Attach the black "hot" wire to the "common terminal" screws at both switches with a screwdriver and needle-nose pliers. These screws are identified with a label or they will be a different color than the other screws.

# Connect your white "traveler" wires to the other screws in the switch. Mark these wires with black electrical tape, cut with an utility knife, to signal that they are hot and not neutral like most wires of this color.
# Attach the bare ground wires to the small screws on each switch. This will ground your circuit.
=== Power to the Light Fixture ===
# Attach the white "hot" wire from the fixture to the "common terminal" screw on the switch at the old location. The black "hot" wire will bypass this switch and continue to the next one.
# Connect the black "hot" wire to the "common terminal" screw on the new switch. The terminal screws for both switches should be labeled or a different color from the others.
#* The red and other white wires should be attached to the other screws on the switch. Remember to mark the white "hot" wires with black tape to indicate they are not neutral.
# Attach the bare ground wires to the small screws on each switch. This will ground your circuit. Turn on the power and test your circuit.
== Warnings ==
* Always make sure the power to the area where you are working is off to avoid electrocution.
* Call a licensed electrician if the wiring in your house is aluminum. The inside of the coating will be light gray instead of copper. You should not work on it yourself.
== Things You'll Need ==
* 14-3 or 12-3 wire cable
* 3-way switches
* Voltage tester (non-contact)
* Screwdriver
* Needle-nose pliers
* Wire stripper
* Black electrical tape
* Utility knife
